newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil wins loan for controversial Amazon highway.
newsitem.headline: Brazil wins loan for controversial Amazon highway.

text.p: A controversial project to pave a highway through the Brazilian Amazon has won international funding, a step some environmentalists say could speed up destruction of the rainforest.

"This road is going to be a disaster," Roberto Kishinami, Greenpeace's executive director in Brazil, said. "It goes right through Indian reservations, various eco-systems, parks and ecological reserves, and it endangers them all."

The Andean Development Corporation, funded by the governments of several Andean nations, agreed on Thursday to loan Brazil $86 million to pave a 390-mile (620-km) stretch of the highway between the jungle city of Manaus and Caracarai, a town in the remote northern state of Roraima.

The funds, to be matched by Brazilian cash, will virtually complete asphalting of the 620-mile (980-km) BR-174 highway from Manaus to the Venezuelan border, half of which remains a dirt road that becomes a muddy quagmire in the rainy season.

One section cuts through the reservation of the remote Waimira-Atroari Indians who last year settled for $3 million in compensation for allowing it on their land after years of opposition and violent clashes with construction teams.

Officials hope completion of the road will open a corridor to the Caribbean and international markets beyond for exports from a tax-free industrial complex in Manaus and for timber. Power lines bringing much-needed Venezuelan electricity to Manaus are planned to accompany the road.

Environmental groups said the paving of highways in other states in the Amazon region had been the catalyst for widespread damage to the forest, caused principally by indiscriminate logging and farming.

"It is fundamental that the highway exists because we're effectively an island surrounded by trees," said Carlos Miller of the Amazon Victory Foundation in Manaus. "But we have to make sure there's no repeat of the usual kind of impact of highways through the Amazon."

The paving of a highway in the state of Rondonia, part of a World Bank-sponsored project in the 1980s, has been widely criticised as a major factor behind explosive deforestation there. One third of Rondonia's forests have now been felled.

Garo Batmanian, executive director in Brazil of the Worldwide Fund for Nature, said he had not yet seen an environmental study for the new highway that took into account the expected influx of migrants. "We know from past experience that paving highways opens up areas for massive occupation. It makes it easier to move in, easier to farm and easier to take timber out," he said.

Kishinami of Greenpeace said he had unsuccessfully urged the Brazilian government to ban any secondary roads leading off the highway and suggested the highway be replaced by a railway to reduce the impact on the rainforest.

A spokesman for the Amazonas state government in Manaus denied the highway represented a threat to the environment. "Ninety-eight percent of our state remains untouched. We can't hold back on development," Julio Cesar Guimaraes said.

He said Amazonas Gov. Amazonino Mendes, who outraged environmentalists by distributing chainsaws to farmers during a previous term, was aware of the importance of sustainable development. "He is a green now," Guimaraes said.
